practice_span: I have been weaving since I was twelve. It has been thirty-one years.
craft_description: I say it is a weave where the dots are tied during the weaving itself. To children I say, this is a cloth made of counting.
craft_distinct: The dot is not stitched on top, it is tied into the weave. So the shawl can be used from both sides.
motif_meaning: The laddu pattern. Its round dots mean happiness and sweetness. White and red on black feel the truest colours.
motif_story: I wove the laddu pattern into a bride's lobadi. At the wedding her mother cried and said, mine had the same.
colour_change: Earlier only black wool with white dots. Now we also weave grey and pink for the city. The dot technique stayed the same.
specialisation: Counting the fine dots. Our group added new geometric patterns and brought women onto the loom.
known_for: People come to me for the fine dots of a bride's lobadi.
craft_keep_change: I would keep the hand-tied dot. I would change selling on credit.
local_belonging_phrase: “Tangaliya belongs to Zalawad. The sisters of our Bharwad brothers wear it, and that is why it has lasted.”
place_belonging_feeling: The Bharwad women of Zalawad kept this cloth alive. That is my pride.
ecological_input: Dry heat makes the yarn brittle, so we set the warp in the morning damp. The sheep's wool used to come only from the pastoralists here.
place_use_moment: One morning I set the warp in the damp air. The yarn did not break and work went well all day.
place_missing: Without the damp, I must wrap the yarn in a wet cloth, and the work slows down.
place_change: A paved road came to the village and the sheep became fewer. Now wool has to be brought from the market, and young people go to powerlooms or the salt pans.
place_before_after: Earlier wool came from the village, now it must come from the market and costs more.
emotion_about_place_change: “I am happy the road brings customers. But when the pastoralists left, our wool left too.”
teacher_name_relation: My father-in-law, Ramjibhai. My parents wove as well, but my father-in-law taught me to tie the dot.
teaching_memory: In my first shawl, one row went crooked. My father-in-law did not undo it. He said, “Finish the whole shawl, then look at that row every day.” My rows have not gone crooked since.
remembered_phrase_gesture: “The dot speaks.” He would tap a dot lightly with one finger, and move on only if it was tight.
family_generations: My father-in-law and his father wove. My husband and I weave. My daughter Komal ties dots, and my son has a job in Surat.
family_line: Father-in-law's father → father-in-law Ramjibhai → me and my husband → daughter Komal.
transmission_strength:
All the women of the house know the dot's knot. Daughters pick it up from childhood just by watching.

The old patterns, especially the counts for lobadi designs. They are not written anywhere, and most stayed in the elders' heads.
teaching_practice: I tie a dot to show, then hold the learner's hand and tie the next one together.
teaching_scene: I sat by the loom on the veranda. My finger was on Komal's finger, and we pulled the knot together.
teaching_difficulty: A shawl takes weeks and the money comes after a month. The young want a daily wage, so they do not sit down to learn.
primary_material:
Sheep's wool, cotton yarn, and thread of a contrasting colour for the fine dots.

Wool used to come from the village pastoralists, now from Ahmedabad and Panipat. Yarn comes from the Surendranagar market.
first_contact: When my mother set the warp, I sat holding the bobbins. At seven, the smell of the wool stayed with me for the first time.
material_special: The dot is tied during the weaving, not embroidered on top. So the shawl can be used from both sides and the dot does not fall out.
material_in_hands: Good yarn pulls back slightly when stretched. When tying a dot, it settles only if it sticks a little to the finger.
material_spoke: When the yarn dries out and creaks, or swells up after the knot, I know something is wrong.
correction_action: I wrap the yarn in a damp cloth overnight. If a knot has swollen, I open it and twist it again, with no hurry.
piece_time: Two to three weeks for one shawl. Never rush tying the dots, or they fall out after washing.
material_change: The village sheep's wool is gone; now we use smooth market wool.
material_change_reason: The pastoralists became fewer and the sheep went down, so the village stopped having wool.
material_change_gain:
Silk and cotton threads make lighter shawls. City customers like them, and they sell in summer too.

The warmth and smell of village wool are gone. Market wool is smooth, but it does not last for years.
occasion_of_use:
The lobadi of Bharwad women, given as a gift at weddings. Also worn at the baby shower and on festival days.

At a wedding the drums play, there is the smell of ghee, and white dots on a black lobadi shine in the evening sun.
use_importance: “You can tell from the lobadi which village the bride is from.” My mother-in-law used to say this.
use_feelings: Weaving a bride's lobadi I feel both pride and responsibility.
special_vs_everyday: The everyday lobadi is plain. A bride's lobadi has dots so fine that it takes a month.
special_object_rule: Before weaving a bride's lobadi we share out jaggery. While weaving it, we do not cut the black warp midway.
special_missing: Without the lobadi at a wedding the bride feels incomplete, and the family is sad.
not_for_sale_example: The family's ‘Dholi’ patterned lobadi, woven only for brides of our community.
why_protected: That pattern is our identity. If it is sold outside it becomes a table cover, and its meaning is gone.
safer_alternative: We have made new patterns for the market: the same dot technique, but geometric designs. Anyone may use photos of those.
pride_source: Turn the shawl over and the dot is still clean. That is the pride of my counting.
pride_moment: At an exhibition in Ahmedabad, a woman weaver turned the shawl over, looked at it, and took my hands without saying a word.
recognition_by_others: That woman, and later our village elder, who said for the first time, “The daughter-in-law has kept the name.”
loss_if_stopped: The whole way of counting with dots would go, and the lobadi of Bharwad brides would be made by machine.
loss_picture: The sound of looms would stop in the village, and brides would wear printed lobadis.
key_stakeholder_of_loss: The daughters of our community and Bharwad families, whose identity is in this cloth.
craft_hours: Six or seven hours a day, counting preparing the yarn. In wedding season we tie dots at night too.
change_in_lifetime: In my childhood the whole lane wove. Today only a few houses remain, but the work now has a name.
artisan_initiated_change: I formed a group of ten women, and women now sit at the loom too. Before, they only tied dots.
desired_keep:
The hand-tied dot, and the old pattern of the bride's lobadi.

Selling on credit, and the belief that only men can sit at the loom.
strength_anchor: I can keep a pattern's count in my fingers without counting the dots. I can get ten women weaving shawls to one measure.
concern_anchor: Printed powerloom copies sell as Tangaliya at half the price, and customers cannot tell the difference.
shareable_content:
The dot technique, the story of our group, photos of the new patterns, and my name.

The count for the bride's lobadi pattern, and details of the group's debts.
desired_change:
Direct orders with half the amount paid first, so we need not borrow for wool.

The dot will be tied by hand. There is no compromise on that.
learning_story: There was a big order and I tied the dots loosely in a hurry. After washing, half fell out. I returned the money, and since that day I wash one corner of every shawl to check.
emotional_story: My father-in-law was in his last days, in bed. I put a shawl in his hands. He could barely see, but he felt the dots with his finger and said, “Now it is all right.”
clarification_story:
A customer asked, this is embroidery, isn't it? I sat them at the loom. Tying two dots took ten minutes, and after that they did not ask about the price.

People think the dots are stitched on top, or that this is only an old tradition. It is everyday mathematics.
